meta.title: Who really said "You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. Eleanor Roosevelt wrote it in You Learn by Living (Harper, 1960), pp. 29–30 — but the longer version online silently cuts three sentences.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Eleanor Roosevelt, You Learn by Living (1960), chapter "Fear—the Great Enemy," pp. 29–30. The popular longer version is spliced.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1884–1962 · First Lady of the United States, 1933–1945; UN Human Rights Commission chair
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Eleanor Roosevelt’s You Learn by Living (Harper & Brothers, New York, 1960), quote pages 29–30, in the chapter “Fear—the Great Enemy.” Quote Investigator transcribed the passage from the printed 1960 book ↗ and Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section at the same pages ↗. This is one of the rare Roosevelt lines that is exactly what it claims to be — though the longer version you usually see online has been quietly cut.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1960 · Harper & Brothers, New York (211 pp., LCCN 60010416)

source.excerpt: You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face. You are able to say to yourself, ‘I lived through this horror. I can take the next thing that comes along.’ The danger lies in refusing to face the fear, in not daring to come to grips with it. If you fail anywhere along the line it will take away your confidence. You must make yourself succeed every time. You must do the thing you think you cannot do.
trail: Quote Investigator quotes the passage and cites it to “1960, You Learn by Living by Eleanor Roosevelt, Quote Page 29 and 30, Harper & Brothers, New York” with the note “Verified on paper” ↗ — a transcription taken from the physical book, not from a quote database.
Wikiquote carries the sentence in its sourced section, under the heading “You Learn by Living (1960),” cited to p. 29–30 ↗ — independent agreement on the same work and the same pages.
Open Library’s catalogue record confirms the first edition: Harper, New York, 1960, 211 pages, LCCN 60010416 ↗, fixing the publication date that the rights question turns on.
The Internet Archive’s scan — a 1983 Westminster Press reprint of the 1960 original — lists “Fear: the great enemy” among its chapters ↗, matching the chapter Quote Investigator names.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed as Quote Investigator gives it from the printed 1960 edition ↗. The version that circulates online drops the three middle sentences and reads “I have lived through this horror”; Wikiquote also prints “I have lived” and marks the omission with an ellipsis ↗.

author.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1884–1962 · First Lady of the United States and UN human rights delegate
author.bio: Anna Eleanor Roosevelt (born 11 October 1884, died 7 November 1962) was First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945 and the first presidential spouse to write a daily syndicated newspaper column, “My Day.” After Franklin Roosevelt’s death she became the first United States Representative to the UN Commission on Human Rights and chaired it, taking a leading role in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted in 1948 — work she regarded as her greatest achievement. You Learn by Living, published by Harper & Brothers in 1960, was a late-life book of practical advice; its second chapter, “Fear—the Great Enemy,” draws directly on what she described as a childhood and early youth spent battling fear.

misattribution.heading: The trouble around a genuine quote
misattribution.intro: This one is real — which is exactly why it causes trouble. A verified Roosevelt passage about facing fear has become the gravitational centre for a fake Roosevelt quote, and the passage itself is almost never quoted as printed.

items.who: “Do one thing every day that scares you”
items.why: This companion line is pinned on Roosevelt constantly, and it is not hers. Quote Investigator concludes that Mary Schmich should receive credit ↗, tracing the exact phrase to her 1 June 1997 Chicago Tribune column ↗, later set to music as Baz Luhrmann’s 1999 “Everybody’s Free (To Wear Sunscreen).” The genuine passage below is the reason the fake sounds plausible.

The circulating version jumps from “I can take the next thing that comes along” directly to “You must do the thing you think you cannot do.” In the printed text three sentences sit between them — about refusing to face fear, about failure costing you confidence, and about making yourself succeed every time. Wikiquote marks the omission with an ellipsis ↗; most quote sites do not.

Our two specialist references do not agree on this inner sentence. Quote Investigator’s transcription, noted as verified on paper, reads “I lived through this horror” ↗, while Wikiquote prints “I have lived through this horror” ↗. We flag the difference rather than pick a winner; it does not affect the headline sentence, on which both agree exactly.

misattribution.truthLine: The famous sentence itself is authentic and precisely locatable: Eleanor Roosevelt, You Learn by Living (Harper & Brothers, 1960), pages 29–30, in the chapter “Fear—the Great Enemy” — transcribed from the printed book by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence reads like a poster slogan, but in the book it is a piece of self-examination. Roosevelt opens the chapter by calling fear the worst stumbling block anyone has to face — “the great crippler” — and says that, looking back, her childhood and early youth were one long battle against it. The advice is not abstract encouragement from a confident woman; it is a report from someone describing how she taught herself to stop flinching.

You Learn by Living appeared in 1960, published by Harper & Brothers in New York. Roosevelt died in November 1962, so the book belongs to the last years of a life that had run from the White House through the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
context.detailsSummary: What the popular version leaves out
detailsBody: The passage that circulates online normally runs the opening sentence, then “I have lived through this horror. I can take the next thing that comes along,” then jumps straight to “You must do the thing you think you cannot do.” Three sentences sit in that gap in the printed book, and they are the demanding ones: the warning that the danger lies in refusing to face the fear, the caution that failing anywhere along the line will take your confidence away, and the instruction that you must make yourself succeed every time.

Wikiquote is honest about the cut and marks it with an ellipsis. Most quote aggregators present the shortened text as continuous prose, which turns a chapter’s argument into a slogan and drops the part that asks something of the reader.
context.pull: You must do the thing you think you cannot do.
